not_claimed: AGY owns implementation. I edited no shared source, no operational unit or DB, and sent nothing to Telegram. The prototype is private and is not a product change.
answer_in_one_line: No new API is needed: hackney.erl ALREADY separates connection creation from connect, so ownership can be taken before any blocking I/O, and the deadline path can use exit(Pid,kill) plus a bounded DOWN instead of the infinity-timeout stop that caused F10.

pinned_path_findings.finding: hackney_conn:init/1 performs NO network I/O. It sets trap_exit, monitors the owner, computes netloc, builds conn_data, and returns {ok, idle, Data} when no pre-established socket is supplied. Connect is a separate exported call.
pinned_path_findings.consequence: The ownership handoff root requires BEFORE any blocking connect is directly available. Creation and connect are already two steps.

pinned_path_findings.finding: hackney.erl itself uses exactly that two-step: hackney_conn_sup:start_conn(ConnOpts) then hackney_conn:connect(ConnPid) or connect(ConnPid, ConnectTimeout).
pinned_path_findings.consequence: The owned protocol is not a reimplementation or a private fork of hackney behaviour. It is the library's own sequence with ownership and a deadline interposed between the two steps. Nothing is invented.

pinned_path_findings.finding: hackney_conn_sup:start_conn/1 is supervisor:start_child(?SERVER, [Opts]), so the connection is NOT linked to the caller. hackney_conn:start_link/1 would link it.
pinned_path_findings.consequence: Use start_conn, not start_link. With start_link, exit(Pid,kill) would send an exit signal back along the link and kill the owner unless it traps exits. start_conn removes that hazard entirely.

pinned_path_findings.finding: owner MUST be passed explicitly in ConnOpts. init/1 resolves Owner as maps:get(owner, Opts, DefaultOwner) where DefaultOwner is the process that called start_link - which, under start_conn, is the SUPERVISOR.
pinned_path_findings.consequence: Omitting owner makes the connection monitor the supervisor instead of the requester, so it would never observe caller death and the orphan-on-caller-death safety net would silently not exist. This is the single easiest thing to get wrong in this design.

pinned_path_findings.evidence: Observed supervisor report during the prototype run: supervisor {local,hackney_conn_sup}, errorContext child_terminated, reason killed, restart_type temporary.
pinned_path_findings.consequence: Killing an owned connection does not trigger a supervisor restart, so a brutal kill on the deadline path cannot cause a restart storm. It does emit a SUPERVISOR REPORT per kill, which is log noise to expect and not an error.

pinned_path_findings.finding: hackney_tcp:connect/4 function_clauses on a BINARY host. It requires a charlist.
pinned_path_findings.evidence: Measured: host as <<"127.0.0.1">> raised function_clause at hackney_tcp.erl:26 via hackney_conn:do_tcp_connect/2 at hackney_conn.erl:2281; host as "127.0.0.1" returned ok.
pinned_path_findings.consequence: Pass the host as a charlist. hackney.erl supplies it that way from URL parsing, so this only bites a direct hackney_conn caller. Without this the whole owned path fails instantly in a way that superficially looks like a connect timeout.

pinned_path_findings.finding: hackney_conn:request/7 returns {ok, Status, Headers} for this path; the body is a separate bounded call (body/1, body/2).
pinned_path_findings.consequence: The deadline must cover a THIRD phase. A design that bounds connect and request only would leave body retrieval unbounded, which is the same shape as F10 one phase later.

protocol.name: owned-connection bounded abort
phases: P0 BOOTSTRAP, once at service start and never per request: application:ensure_all_started(hackney). It must not consume a request budget, and it must be bounded and owned by the service start path.
P1 CREATE AND OWN, no I/O: {ok, ConnPid} = hackney_conn_sup:start_conn(ConnOpts#{owner => OwnerPid}). Host as charlist (H6). owner explicit (H4).

P2 MONITOR AND RECORD, before any blocking call: Ref = monitor(process, ConnPid), then persist the pending context {request_id, ConnPid, Ref, Deadline, commit_state} so an abandoned request is recoverable. This ordering is the whole point: the parent holds the exact pid and monitor before the first byte moves.
P3 CONNECT, bounded by remaining deadline: hackney_conn:connect(ConnPid, Remaining).
P4 REQUEST, bounded by remaining deadline: hackney_conn:request(ConnPid, Method, Path, Headers, Body, Remaining, ReqOpts).
P5 BODY, bounded by remaining deadline: hackney_conn:body(ConnPid, Remaining) (H7).
P6 TERMINATE OWNED, on every exit path: exit(ConnPid, kill), then receive the matching {'DOWN', Ref, process, ConnPid, _} with a bounded after, then demonitor(Ref,[flush]).
protocol.gen_statem_call_hazard: connect/2, request/7 and body/2 are gen_statem:call, which EXITS the caller on timeout rather than returning an error. Every one must be wrapped so that exit:{timeout,_} becomes a typed abort. An unwrapped call turns a deadline into a caller crash.
protocol.no_infinity_stop: hackney_conn:stop/1 and hackney:close/1 are NOT used on the deadline path. That is the F10 repair: hackney:close descends to hackney_conn:stop -> proc_lib:stop -> gen:do_call with a default infinity timeout, which blocked over 1500 ms under an 80 ms configuration.
protocol.scope_discipline: Only ConnPid is ever signalled. No connection enumeration, no pool sweep, no killing of unrelated connections. The owned pid is known from P1.
caller_death_and_races: Caller dies after P1: the connection monitors the owner (H4), observes DOWN, and terminates itself. This is the safety net for the window between start_conn and P2, and it exists only if owner was passed explicitly.
Connection dies before the deadline: the DOWN is already queued, exit/2 on a dead pid is a no-op, and P6 receives the queued DOWN. No special case needed.

Deadline fires concurrently with a successful reply: the reply is taken if already matched, otherwise the abort path runs and the request is reported uncertain. The outcome must be uncertain, not failed, because the peer may have acted.
DOWN does not arrive within the abort budget: report down_not_confirmed explicitly rather than assuming success. A kill that cannot be confirmed is an observability failure and must be visible.
preserved_policies: Host header: computed by compute_netloc(Host, Port, Transport) inside hackney_conn:init/1, so it is preserved by construction rather than reimplemented.
TLS verification: pass ssl_options through ConnOpts exactly as hackney.erl does (observed at hackney.erl lines 116, 233, 372, 642). Do not substitute defaults.
Content length: taken from response headers as returned by request/7; the existing max-bytes bound continues to apply to the body phase.

Redirects: follow_redirect defaults to false and max_redirect to 5 in hackney.erl lines 794-795. The current UOS FFI does not enable redirects, so the owned path loses no redirect behaviour. If redirects are ever wanted they must be implemented over this protocol deliberately, because hackney.erl's follow_redirect/N is bypassed.
Transport selection: unchanged; pass hackney_tcp or the TLS transport as hackney.erl does.

aggregate: hygiene=true success_case_ok=true aborts_are_errors=true, OWNED_ABORT_PROTOTYPE pass=true
prototype.relation_to_root_orphan_finding: Root's service_http_orphan.erl proved the connection was still ALIVE 150 ms after the call returned, with the server having written 67 bytes over 1569 ms. The prototype reports alive_after_return=false and down_confirmed on all three cases INCLUDING the success path, which is the direct repair for that finding. Termination is applied on both paths because no pooling or reuse is in use here.
preserved_failures: First run: all three cases returned errors in 0-22 ms because the host was passed as a binary. Root cause H6 (hackney_tcp:connect/4 function_clause on a binary host). Preserved because the symptom superficially resembled a connect timeout and would have been easy to misread as a bound working.

First run also PASSED its own aggregate predicate while every request had failed, because the predicate checked only bounded + DOWN + not-alive and never checked that the success case succeeded. This is the same defect class recorded in CLAUDE_SERVICE_REVIEW F2 - an observable coarser than the property - committed by me in my own test. The predicate was split into three independent gates (hygiene, success_case_ok, aborts_are_errors) and all three are now asserted.
A diagnostic module named dbg collided with OTP's built-in dbg and was undefined at call time; renamed to abort_dbg.

serve_silent emits a badmatch on {error,closed} from gen_tcp:recv AFTER the assertion, because killing the owned connection closes the socket under the fixture. Fixture noise, not a protocol failure; recorded rather than silenced.
Each kill emits a SUPERVISOR REPORT (child_terminated, reason killed, restart_type temporary). Expected; see H5.

positive: A complete valid response returns 200 with the expected body within the deadline, and the owned connection is confirmed dead after return.
refusal: Valid fragmented headers under an 80 ms configuration return within 80 ms plus the abort budget, not over 1500 ms. This is root's cleanup2 case.
A peer that accepts TCP and never writes is bounded at the deadline.
A slow body drip of 1-byte chunks is bounded by the deadline, not by max bytes.
Elapsed wall time never exceeds deadline plus abort budget plus tolerance across every fixture. Assert on ELAPSED TIME, never on the returned classification.
crash: After any abort, is_process_alive(ConnPid) is false and the DOWN was confirmed.
The caller mailbox contains no residual connection message after abort.
Killing the caller between create and monitor leaves no orphan, via the owner monitor in H4.
No connection other than the owned pid is signalled during any case.
bootstrap: With hackney not yet started, the first request either returns within its deadline or fails closed, proving bootstrap is not inside the request budget.

unknowns: U-1 I did not test TLS. All three cases are plaintext hackney_tcp against 127.0.0.1. The ssl_options pass-through is read from hackney.erl, not exercised, so TLS verification behaviour under the owned path is UNVERIFIED.

U-2 I did not test HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. hackney 3.2.1 contains hackney_http2 and hackney_h3 and separate checkout_h2 and checkout_h3 paths in hackney.erl; whether the owned protocol composes with protocol negotiation is UNKNOWN.

U-3 I did not test against a pooled configuration. The current UOS FFI passes {pool,false} and the prototype uses none, so interaction with hackney_pool and release_to_pool is UNKNOWN. Terminating on the success path is correct only while there is no reuse.

U-4 request_async/6..9 plus stream_next/1 were not used. The current UOS FFI uses {async, once} streaming, so the owned protocol as prototyped changes the response-reading style from async streaming to bounded synchronous calls. The max-bytes bound currently enforced incrementally during chunk accumulation would need to be re-established on the body phase, and I did NOT demonstrate that.
U-5 The 250 ms abort budget is a chosen value with no measurement behind it. Observed DOWN latency was well inside it, but the value is not justified by evidence.
U-6 I did not measure whether repeated kills leak file descriptors or ETS entries over a long run.

U-7 Whether this protocol belongs in the FFI or behind a Gleam-owned worker process is a placement decision I did not settle. CLAUDE_SERVICE_REVIEW F8R calls for an owner process with cancellation; this protocol supplies the cancellation primitive that such an owner would use.

safer_existing_alternative_considered.option: Keep hackney:request/5 with {async, once} and wrap the whole call in a monitored child process that the owner kills at the deadline.
safer_existing_alternative_considered.assessment: Simpler and preserves the current streaming and incremental max-bytes behaviour, but it does NOT satisfy the requirement: the connection is created inside hackney:request, so at kill time the parent still does not know the exact connection pid and cannot confirm its death. Root's orphan finding is precisely that the connection outlives the return. Killing a wrapper child abandons the connection rather than reaping it.
safer_existing_alternative_considered.conclusion: The owned protocol is preferred because it is the only one of the two that can name and confirm the death of the exact connection. It costs the switch from async streaming to bounded synchronous phases, which is U-4.
